column8:
Where imagination finds shelter.
This is not built into a tree-it is grown with it. A structure shaped and integrated with living branches, the tree house here is not separate from nature but continuous with it.
It asks a question: what if the built world didn't just sit on the land, but grew from it? What if architecture could be patient, adaptive, alive?
Climb if you can. Look out from within the canopy.
Some of our oldest dreams-of sheltering in trees, of living close to the sky-are here, made real.
column11:
- A second, distinct installation exists on-site: a living sculpture where tree trunks and branches are trained into the architectural silhouette of a house

column12:
Most sculptures are made from dead things. Stone, cut timber, cast metal, and clay. The Living Tree House is made from none of these. Living trees make up its trunks, its branches, and its walls. All still growing.

The structure itself tells a stranger story.

These trunks and branches have been guided, branch by branch, into the shape of a house. The technique is called arborsculpture.

This is just the beginning. The next phase will bring fully enclosed living rooms that visitors can walk inside.

A house that grows, that breathes, and that will keep changing long after today.

column8:
Where wish meets root.
In Hindu mythology, the Kalpavriksha is the wish-fulfilling tree-a divine tree capable of granting whatever the pure of heart desires. It represents the abundance of nature and the power of intention aligned with the natural world.
This tree, planted as a living symbol, carries that tradition forward. It asks not for worship but for awareness: that what we grow toward matters, and that the earth, tended with care, gives back in kind.
Stand beneath it quietly. Hold whatever you are carrying.
Not all wishes need to be spoken aloud. Sometimes, to name what you need in the presence of something ancient is enough.
column11:
- Approximately 1,500 years old

- Transported from Africa by sea — many months at sea, in iced containers
- Seven Baobab species exist worldwide; six are native to Africa, one to Australia
- Trunks can grow up to 20 feet in diameter

column12:
These three Baobabs come from Africa. Here at Experium, they are called Kalpavriksha. They have been alive for one thousand five hundred years.

The park transported them across the ocean. They traveled for many months at sea, kept alive inside iced containers. Seven Baobab species exist in the world. Six of them come from Africa.

For fifteen centuries, these trees survived earthquakes, thunderstorms, forest fires, pests, and human encroachment. The park calls that endurance self power. Their trunks can grow up to twenty feet wide.

This exhibit is designed for touch. Visitors are invited to step forward, hold the trunks, and feel the calm that fifteen centuries and an ocean have pressed into the bark.

column8:
Where stillness moves.
This figure is not seated in classic meditation-it is moving. And yet the quality of presence it carries is unmistakable: a calm that does not depend on stillness, an awareness that travels with the body rather than requiring the body to stop.
This is a different kind of teaching: that presence is not confined to the meditation cushion. That the qualities we associate with stillness-attention, ease, openness-can be practiced in motion.
Watch the figure. Then notice your own body.
You are always already in motion. The question is whether you are present within it.

column12:
In a forest in Indonesia, a tree took root on solid stone. No soil. No help. Just roots gripping rock.

This is the Lotus Tree. A stone-rooted tree hand-shaped into the outline of an open lotus flower, with a Buddha statue resting inside its hollow center.

A nursery owner found it growing on a rock in Indonesia and nurtured it. The park's founder discovered it there and brought it here. The tree alone cost ₹85 lakhs. The journey added ₹5 lakhs. The hand-crafted Buddha inside the tree is valued at ₹15 lakhs.

That lotus shape was not natural. It was guided into existence, one branch at a time. The Lotus Tree is still growing. Its branches are still being shaped, even today.

column12:
Forty years ago, someone planted a chair.

Not carved. Not cut. Planted, and trained to grow into this shape.

These living chairs came from Indonesia, grown by a craftsman who spent four decades patiently bending and shaping living trees into functional seats. The craftsman was regarded as an artist. Experium acquired these directly from his grandson.

Most furniture begins with a fallen tree. These chairs never let the tree fall.

Each one cost twelve and a half lakhs. That is about the price of a fine painting made in a single day. But a painting stops when the artist puts down the brush. These chairs are still growing.

column4:
* **Origin:** Imported from Papua New Guinea.


* **Exclusivity:** Described as the only trees of their kind in India.


* **Cost:** Approximately 14 lakhs per tree.


* **Appearance:** The trunks develop multi-colored rainbow patterns upon reaching maturity; while some colors are visible now, they fully develop within 2 to 5 years.

column8:
A living canvas of transformation.
This tree paints itself in time. Its bark gently sheds in flowing layers, revealing fresh green that slowly deepens into blues, purples, amber, and maroon. What you see is not pigment, but life unfolding- shaped by light, air, and growth.
Each color is a moment. Each layer, a quiet becoming. In shedding, it renews. In exposure, it evolves.
Rooted in tropical abundance, it thrives in warmth and moisture, rising tall like a natural tower-ever- growing, ever-changing.

Pause here. Breathe. Observe.
Nature is not still-it is becoming.
And so are you.
column11:

column12:
Look at the trunk. The colors aren't painted. The tree makes them itself.

This is the Rainbow Eucalyptus forest. These are the only trees of their kind in India. Every single one was brought here from Papua New Guinea. Each one cost fourteen lakhs.

Right now, you can already see the colors beginning to appear. The trunks keep developing their rainbow pattern as they mature. The full display takes two to five years. Every time you visit, this forest looks a little different.

Without trimming, these trees would reach 120 feet. Experium keeps them at a height you can actually take in.

column12: Touch this trunk and your hand comes away golden. This is the Namibian Gold Powder Tree. The only one of its kind in all of India. Native to Namibia, the bark is coated in a fine, natural golden powder. Press your palm against it and the gold transfers to your skin. Across parts of Africa, local communities have gathered this golden powder for generations. Not as a dye. Not as medicine. As talcum powder. A soft, natural dusting powder, taken straight from the tree. No processing needed. The tree simply makes it. Every day, without being asked. It is a living, golden tree. column12:
What you're looking at was once a living tree. Today, every inch of it is solid stone.

This is fossil wood. It is the tallest piece in the park's fossil wood collection. Ten million years ago, a tree fell. Over time, its wood dissolved, mineral by mineral, and was replaced by rock. The original shape survived. The cells survived. The tree became stone. It has stayed that way ever since.

The founder sourced this piece from overseas. At roughly fifteen lakh rupees per piece, the park holds several of these ancient stones. Each one came from a different country.

Ten million years of time, preserved in something you can stand next to.

column8:
Where aspiration takes root.
Named for the ideals it embodies-strength, endurance, and the pursuit of excellence-this tree stands as a living symbol of what we are capable of when we commit to growth.
In many traditions, specific trees mark significant events: planted at births, dedicated to achievements, grown as living memorials. This one carries that same intention-a marker of human aspiration held in living form.
Stand here a moment.
What are you growing toward? What would you plant today that you hope to stand beneath one day?
column11:

column12:
Look at those rings. Not carved. Not painted. Grown.

This is the Olympic Tree. Its branches have been trained, year by year, into the shape of the five interlocking Olympic rings.

It came from China, shaped by a single nurseryman as a personal tribute to the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing. Experium brought it here for nearly eighty lakh rupees. Because there is nothing else like it in the world.

What you see isn't finished. The tree is alive. Every day, its branches press outward. Every day, a careful hand guides them back into those five perfect circles.

One person. Years of patience. A living memory of the Olympics, still growing.

Where the path rises.
This is not just a walk-it is a perspective shift. Elevated above the ground, you move through the middle story of the forest-a realm normally unseen, where branches spread, light filters differently, and the sounds of the canopy replace those of the ground.
From here, familiar things look new. The forest is not below you-you are inside it.
Move slowly. Let the height change your relationship to the trees.
Sometimes, to understand a place, you have to change your level within it.

column12:
What's above you has never existed anywhere else on Earth. Not like this.

This is the Living Canopy Pavilion. The world's first man-made living canopy of its kind. Already on its way to a Guinness World Record.

Living plants have been cultivated and trained across an overhead framework. Slowly, the plants reach outward, filling in gaps, and building toward complete shade. In six months to a year, every inch of sky above this space will be covered in green.

Right now, you are standing inside something still becoming. A family gathering spot, a concert venue, and a cool, shaded retreat. All growing into place above you.

column8:
Where form holds meaning.
This tree does not just grow-it holds. Its form, like a vessel, creates interior space: a cup, a container, a place where things can gather. Water pools in its curves. Birds rest in its hollows. Light collects in the spaces its branches define.
To call something a vessel is to say: it is shaped by what it carries. Over time, this tree has been shaped by the weight of seasons, the pull of light, the passage of wind. Its form is a record of everything it has received.
Look into it, not just at it.
What are you carrying? What shape has it given you?

This is a tree. It grew from a seed. And someone spent thirty years turning it into a kettle.

The Kettle Tree — the only one of its form in India. A master artist from Southeast Asia trained this living tree, branch by patient branch, into the silhouette of a kettle. Not once did they carve it or cut it into shape. They simply guided it, year after year.

It was brought to Experium for ₹65 lakhs. The founder wanted something that could not be copied overnight.

Today, this tree sets the standard for every living sculpture in the park. It's still alive. Still growing. Still a kettle.

Information Panel Copy (Signage Ready)The Grand Penjing GardenWhile traditional bonsai focuses on shaping miniature individual trees, the ancient art of Penjing combines dwarfed trees with stone elements to recreate comprehensive natural landscapes in miniature. Widely celebrated in international competitions across Southeast Asia and Japan, this installation represents the world's largest dedicated Penjing garden, spanning a 1-acre footprint.   Designed in collaboration with an award-winning master Penjing artist from Vietnam, the exhibit showcases intricate tray landscapes—frequently composed within oval vessels measuring 2 by 1.5 feet and 1.5 by 1 foot. This extensive miniature art collection is anchored within a grander environment featuring rare geological stones, artistic sculptures, and ancient olive trees.
column8:
Where scale dissolves.
In this garden, entire landscapes are held in miniature-mountains, rivers, forests, and paths compressed into living compositions. Each piece is a world unto itself, shaped over years, sometimes decades.
Penjing is not decoration-it is meditation in form. Every leaf, every branch, every mossy stone is placed with care, shaped by patience, and animated by the passage of time.
Lean in. Look closely.
What seems small contains multitudes. And in its quiet precision, it asks you to slow down long enough to see.
column11:
- Penjing is distinct from standalone bonsai: it integrates miniature trees with water and stone elements inside oval vessels to depict complete natural landscapes
- Display vessels are oval-shaped shallow bowls/trays
- Specimen dimensions: miniature trees and stone compositions measuring 2 ft × 1.5 ft and 1.5 ft × 1 ft
- The garden covers approximately 1 acre
- Master planned and crafted by an award-winning Penjing artist from Vietnam
- Bonsai plant specimens are cultivated in miniature tree forms
- Ancient/very old olive trees (Olea europaea) are present in the garden
- Natural materials include small landscaping stones, rare geological stones, and sculptural pieces
- The compositional layout blends miniature potted landscapes with mature monumental features (aged olive trees, rare stones, curated sculptures)
- Cultural origin: prominent horticultural art form across Japan and Southeast Asia
- Exhibition standards are aligned with international competitive Penjing exhibition criteria practiced across Southeast Asia and Japan
column12:
The world's largest collection of the world's smallest landscapes is right here.

This is the Penjing Garden. It stretches across one full acre of Experium, and every inch is packed with miniature worlds.

Penjing is different from bonsai. Bonsai shapes a single tree. Penjing builds an entire natural scene inside a shallow oval tray. Trees, stones, and water together. Rare stones become cliffs. A tiny trunk becomes a forest.

An award-winning Penjing master from Vietnam designed every piece here. Some trays are just two feet wide. Each one is a complete landscape, shaped to meet the standards of international Penjing competitions.

Ancient olive trees stand over the garden, a living frame for the miniature worlds below.
